Isaiah says: you will weep no more. How gracious He will be when you cry for help! As soon as He hears, He will answer you. When you cry, the response is grace, not irritation.

Cry for help today. You'll be met with kindness.

en.verse: I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will guide him and restore comfort to him and his mourners.
en.note:
Your whole family is grieving. Everyone around you is sad, and you're not sure where comfort will come from.

Shared grief can be both comforting and overwhelming. Everyone needs support at once.

God says through Isaiah: I will guide them and restore comfort to Israel's mourners. Not just to the one who's hurting, but to everyone mourning with them.

Healing comes to whole families, whole circles of grief. You and the people sad with you are all in view.

en.verse: I will rejoice in Jerusalem and take delight in My people. The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her.
en.note:
You can't imagine a world without tears. Sadness seems to be everywhere.

When we're in deep grief, it can seem like sadness is just how the world is.

Isaiah describes a renewed world: the sound of weeping and of crying will be heard in it no more. A city where no one cries.

Today there might be tears. But they're not the final sound. Joy is. Hold onto that picture of the future.

en.verse: My sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me.
en.note:
Your sorrow feels beyond healing. You can't imagine it ever getting better.

Deep grief can feel permanent. We can't see past it.

Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet. He watched his nation fall and didn't hide his sadness: my sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me. He said it plainly.

If you feel your sorrow is beyond healing today, Jeremiah felt it too. And God didn't leave him. You're in honest company.

en.verse: This is what the LORD says: “Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for the reward for your work will come, declares the LORD. Then your children will return from the land of the enemy.”
en.note:
You wonder if all your love and effort was wasted. You loved, you tried, and still you lost.

After loss, it's easy to feel that what we gave was for nothing.

God says through Jeremiah: restrain your voice from weeping, for your work will be rewarded. Your grief, your love, your effort: none of it was wasted.

Something will come from it. Not today, maybe. But the reward is real.

en.verse: For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears. For there is no one nearby to comfort me, no one to revive my soul. My children are destitute because the enemy has prevailed.
en.note:
There's no one near you right now. No one to sit with you in this.

Grief is lonely. Sometimes the people we need most aren't there.

Lamentations doesn't hide that: this is why I weep and my eyes overflow with tears. No one is near to comfort me, no one to restore my spirit.

If there's no one near you today, say so to God. And if you can, tell one person. Let them come near.

en.verse: My soul has been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is.
en.note:
You've been sad so long you've forgotten what good days feel like.

Long sadness can erase our memory of happiness. We forget it was ever different.

The writer says: I have been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is. And then, a few verses later: yet this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope.

If you've forgotten good days, you're not broken. You're tired. Try calling one good memory to mind today.

en.verse: As she stood behind Him at His feet weeping, she began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair. Then she kissed His feet and anointed them with the perfume.
en.note:
You're crying in front of people, and you're afraid of what they'll think.

We often feel ashamed of tears, especially in public.

A woman with a bad reputation came into a dinner party and wept at Jesus' feet, wiping them with her hair. Everyone at the table judged her. Jesus defended her, and said her love was great.

Your tears are welcome, even if others don't understand them. Jesus didn't turn away from hers.

en.verse: As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it.
en.note:
You're sad about the state of the world, about people who can't see what they're losing. And you wonder if God cares.

Sometimes our sadness isn't personal. It's grief for others, for the world.

Jesus approached Jerusalem and, seeing the city, wept over it. He cried over a city that didn't understand what it was missing.

God isn't untouched by sadness. He weeps too. Your grief for the world isn't something He stands outside of.

en.verse: And he went outside and wept bitterly.
en.note:
You're sad because of something you did. Regret mixed with sorrow.

Sadness that comes from our own failures is especially painful. We feel we deserve it.

Peter, right after denying Jesus three times, went outside and wept bitterly. Sadness mixed with regret. But this isn't the end of Peter's story. Jesus later found him, asked him three times "do you love Me?" and gave him a purpose again.

Your regret isn't the end of your story either.

en.verse: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.
en.note:
You wonder if your sadness matters to God, especially if He knows how everything will turn out.

We sometimes think that if God knows the ending, He wouldn't be moved by our pain now.

Jesus stood with Mary as she wept over her brother Lazarus. He was deeply moved and troubled. He knew He was about to raise Lazarus, and He was still moved.

Your sadness moves Him, even when He knows how the story ends.

en.verse: Instead, your hearts are filled with sorrow because I have told you these things.
en.note:
You're sad, and no one has even noticed. Or if they have, they haven't said anything.

Being seen in sadness matters. Being named matters.

Jesus said at the Last Supper, looking at His friends: because I have said these things, you are filled with grief. He noticed. He named it. Before He comforted them, He saw them.

Your sorrow is seen first. Let that be a small comfort today.

en.verse: We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.
en.note:
You're sad about the world. The news, injustice, suffering. People tell you not to take it so hard.

Some people feel the world's pain deeply. It's not oversensitivity. It's empathy.

Paul writes: the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth. Not just you. Everything groans, waiting for things to be made right. And childbirth pain leads to new life.

If you're sad about the world, you're feeling what creation feels. And it's groaning toward something new.

en.verse: Sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
en.note:
You're sad, and you feel guilty for also feeling glad about some things. Shouldn't you be one or the other?

We often think emotions have to be pure: either sad or happy.

Paul writes: sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Both at once. He doesn't say sadness disappears. He says joy can live alongside it.

You can be sad today and still find one thing to be glad about. They can share the same heart.

en.verse: Then she went off and sat down nearby, about a bowshot away, for she said, “I cannot bear to watch the boy die!” And as she sat nearby, she lifted up her voice and wept.
en.note:
You can't bear to look at your situation. It's too painful. So you've turned away.

Sometimes grief is so heavy we can't face it directly.

Hagar and her son were sent into the desert with nothing. When the water ran out, she put her son under a bush, sat a distance away, and wept: I can't watch the boy die. And the very next verse says: God heard the boy crying.

Even when you can't bear to look, God is still looking. And listening.

en.verse: Then Joseph fell upon his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him.
en.note:
You feel weak for grieving so hard. You're supposed to be the strong one.

Many people believe grief is weakness, especially for those who carry responsibility.

Joseph was the most powerful man in Egypt. When his father Jacob died, Joseph threw himself on his father and wept over him and kissed him.

Grief isn't weakness. It's love that has nowhere to go. Even the strongest people cry.

en.verse: In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears.
en.note:
Your prayers are messy. Desperate, tearful, not at all composed. You wonder if that's okay.

We sometimes think prayer should be calm and orderly.

Hannah had longed for a child for years. In deep anguish, she prayed to the LORD, weeping bitterly. She prayed so intensely that the priest thought she was drunk.

You can pray like that too. Messy, desperate, honest. God heard Hannah. He hears you.

en.verse: The king was shaken and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he walked, he cried out, “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!”
en.note:
Your grief is complicated. Mixed with anger, regret, love, all tangled together.

Grief isn't always clean. Sometimes we grieve people who hurt us, or relationships that were broken.

David's son Absalom had betrayed him, tried to take his throne, and died in battle. And David wept: O my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you! He grieved as if the betrayal didn't matter.

Complicated grief is still grief. Let yourself feel all of it.

en.verse: “Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.”
en.note:
Sadness has changed how you see yourself. You feel bitter, like that's who you are now.

Long sorrow can reshape our identity. We start to define ourselves by our loss.

Naomi lost her husband and both sons. When she returned home, she said: don't call me Naomi (pleasant). Call me Mara (bitter). She changed her name. But by the end of the book of Ruth, she's holding a grandson in her lap.

Bitter isn't the last name you'll carry.

en.verse: Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was.
en.note:
Someone you love is grieving, and you don't know what to say. So you're staying away.

We often avoid grieving people because we're afraid of saying the wrong thing.

When Job's friends heard about his suffering, they came and sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word, because they saw how great his suffering was. Later they talked and ruined it. But those first seven silent days were their best.

Sometimes presence is better than words. Just show up.

en.verse: My friends are my scoffers as my eyes pour out tears to God.
en.note:
The people around you don't understand your sadness. Some even mock it, or tell you to get over it.

When others dismiss our grief, it doubles the pain.

Job says: my intercessor is my friend as my eyes pour out tears to God. His friends had turned against him, but he still brought his tears to God.

When the people around you don't understand, you can still bring your tears to God. He won't scoff. He'll listen.

en.verse: “Please, Lord,” Moses replied, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue.”
en.note:
There's something about you that you see as a real weakness. Not imagined. Real.

Sometimes our inadequacy isn't just a feeling. There really is something we're not good at.

Moses said: I have never been eloquent. I am slow of speech and tongue. God didn't deny it. He said in the next verse: who gave man his mouth? I will help you.

Your weakness can be real. So is the help. You don't have to fix the weakness first.

en.verse: But Moses asked God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?”
en.note:
"Who am I to do this?" The question keeps coming back. You feel too small for what you're being asked to do.

This is one of the most common questions people ask when facing something big.

Moses asked exactly this: who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh? And God's answer wasn't "you're amazing." It was: I will be with you. Who you are matters less than who's with you.

Next time you ask "who am I?", hear that answer. You won't be doing it alone.

en.verse: “Please, my Lord,” Gideon replied, “how can I save Israel? Indeed, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house.”
en.note:
You have a long list of reasons why you're not the right person. Too young, too inexperienced, not from the right background.

We can be very good at disqualifying ourselves.

Gideon listed every reason: my clan is the weakest, and I am the least in my family. And God ignored the list. The next verse: I will be with you.

God sees something you don't. Your list of inadequacies isn't the final word.

en.verse: And Samuel asked him, “Are these all the sons you have?” “There is still the youngest,” Jesse replied, “but he is tending the sheep.” “Send for him,” Samuel replied. “For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.”
en.note:
People overlook you. Even your own family. You're not the one they think of first.

Being overlooked by people close to us is a deep hurt.

When the prophet Samuel came to anoint a king from among Jesse's sons, Jesse didn't even call David in from the sheep. He was overlooked by his own father. And he was the one God chose.

Being overlooked by people doesn't mean being overlooked by God.

en.verse: David added, “The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine.” “Go,” said Saul, “and may the LORD be with you.”
en.note:
You're facing something big and you don't think you've done anything to prepare for it.

We often forget the small victories that built our strength. They happened quietly, and we don't count them.

David volunteered to fight Goliath. His confidence came from remembering: the LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the bear will rescue me now. Small, unseen victories in a field with sheep.

What's a small victory you've forgotten? It's evidence for today.

en.verse: Then King David went in, sat before the LORD, and said, “Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?”
en.note:
You can't believe where you are. It feels like you don't deserve it, like you got here by accident.

Feeling small can sometimes be the beginning of something good: gratitude.

David, now king, sat before God and said: who am I, Sovereign LORD, that You have brought me this far? He was still amazed he'd been chosen.

Look how far you've been brought. Feeling small isn't always bad. Sometimes it's the beginning of thanks.

en.verse: And now, O LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in my father David’s place. But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in.
en.note:
You've been given a responsibility, and honestly, you have no idea what you're doing.

We often hide our uncertainty, afraid of being exposed.

Solomon, newly crowned king, prayed: I am only a little child and do not know how to carry out my duties. He admitted he didn't know. And he asked for wisdom. God loved that answer.

Admitting you don't know is where wisdom starts. Ask for it today.

en.verse: “Ah, Lord GOD,” I said, “I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!”
en.note:
You feel unready. Too young, too inexperienced. You want to wait until you're more prepared.

Every generation has people who feel this way. Waiting until we feel fully ready often means waiting forever.

Jeremiah said: I do not know how to speak; I am too young. His excuse was his youth. God's answer, in the next verse: don't say that. Go.

You might not feel ready. You might not need to.

en.verse: “Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you,” declares the LORD.
en.note:
You're afraid of the people you'll have to face. Their judgment, their reaction.

Fear of others' reactions can keep us from doing what we're called to.

God said to Jeremiah: do not be afraid of them, for I am with you and will rescue you. Jeremiah felt too young and unqualified. God didn't give him more qualifications. He gave him company.

You might not feel ready. You won't be alone.

en.verse: Then I said: “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.”
en.note:
You feel unworthy. Like if God really saw you, He'd turn away.

That feeling is old, honest, and shared by prophets.

Isaiah saw a vision of God and immediately said: woe to me! I am ruined, for I am a man of unclean lips. He felt completely unworthy. But read on: the next thing that happens is not rejection. It's cleansing.

If you feel unworthy today, you might be in the moment just before being made clean.

en.verse: And with it he touched my mouth and said: “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.”
en.note:
You've been carrying a sense of being unclean, unworthy. Like something about you needs to be fixed before you're acceptable.

Shame often tells us we have to clean ourselves up before we can come close.

After Isaiah cried out that he was unworthy, an angel flew to him with a live coal from the altar, touched his lips, and said: your guilt is taken away and your sin atoned for. Isaiah didn't fix himself. He was made clean. Then he was sent.

If you feel unworthy today, you don't have to clean yourself up first. You can be made clean.

en.verse: “Do not fear, O Jacob, you worm, O few men of Israel. I will help you,” declares the LORD. “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.”
en.note:
You feel tiny. Insignificant. Like a worm, if you're honest.

When we feel small, we often assume we're beneath God's notice.

God says through Isaiah: do not be afraid, you worm Jacob, little Israel, for I Myself will help you. It sounds insulting, but it's tender: God calls them by how small they feel, and then says: I will help you.

You don't have to feel big to be helped. Even if you feel like a worm today, you're His.

en.verse: But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent My strength in futility and vanity; yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God.”
en.note:
You've worked so hard, and it feels like nothing came of it. All that effort, for what?

When effort seems wasted, we start to question our worth.

This is the voice of God's servant in Isaiah: I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing at all. Yet what is due me is in the LORD's hand. Feeling like your effort went nowhere, and still trusting it's held somewhere.

Not every result is visible. Your work counts more than you can see.

en.verse: You have given me Your shield of salvation; Your right hand upholds me, and Your gentleness exalts me.
en.note:
You've been hard on yourself. Critical, demanding, never satisfied. Pushing yourself to be better through sheer pressure.

We often think harshness will make us grow. But people usually grow better under gentleness.

David writes: You make Your saving help my shield; Your right hand sustains me; Your gentleness exalts me. Not God's power, not His strictness: His gentleness. That's what lifted David up.

If you've been hard on yourself, notice that it's gentleness that grows people. Try being gentle with yourself today.

en.verse: For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He adorns the afflicted with salvation.
en.note:
You feel plain. Unremarkable. Nothing special about you.

In a world that celebrates the extraordinary, ordinary can feel like failure.

The psalmist writes: the LORD takes delight in His people; He crowns the humble with victory. Takes delight. Not tolerates. And He dresses the humble in beauty.

You might feel plain or small today. You're delighted in. And adorned.

en.verse: Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
en.note:
You feel like you don't measure up. Not attractive enough, not charming enough, not impressive enough.

The world constantly measures us by appearance and charm. It's exhausting to keep up.

This proverb is part of a poem about a woman of strength: charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. What the world measures you by fades. What lasts is a heart turned toward God.

If you feel inadequate by the world's measures, you're using the wrong ruler.

en.verse: Behold, at that time, I will deal with all who afflict you. I will save the lame and gather the scattered; and I will appoint praise and fame for the disgraced throughout the earth.
en.note:
You've been shamed. Laughed at, put down, made to feel small. And it still stings.

Shame can stay with us long after the moment passes.

God says through Zephaniah: I will rescue the lame; I will gather the exiles. I will give them praise and honor in every land where they have suffered shame. The ones who limp, the ones who've been shamed: they get honor.

God turns things upside down. Your shame isn't permanent.

en.verse: Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
en.note:
You feel like you're at the bottom of the spiritual ladder. Others are so much further along.

We often rank ourselves against others, and we usually rank ourselves low.

Jesus said John the Baptist was the greatest person ever born. And yet, He added, whoever is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. In God's kingdom, "least" doesn't mean worthless. It means you're in.

And being in is everything. You don't need to be higher on the ladder.

en.verse: His master replied, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’
en.note:
Your responsibilities feel small. Not much to show for your life.

We often think only big achievements matter.

In Jesus' story, a master returns and praises a servant: well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. A few things. Small responsibilities. And they're celebrated.

You don't need to do huge things to hear "well done." Be faithful with your few things today.

en.verse: Sitting down, Jesus called the Twelve and said, “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.”
en.note:
You serve others quietly, and no one notices. You feel unimportant.

In a world that rewards visibility, quiet service can feel invisible.

The disciples were arguing about which of them was the greatest. Jesus sat down and said: anyone who wants to be first must be the very last, and the servant of all.

In God's way of seeing, the ones who serve quietly are the great ones. You're closer to greatness than you think.

en.verse: When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees. “Go away from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man.”
en.note:
You feel unworthy to be near God. Too sinful, too messy, too far gone.

Shame often makes us want to push away the very help we need.

After a miraculous catch of fish, Peter fell at Jesus' knees and said: go away from me, Lord; I am a sinful man! His first reaction to Jesus' power was shame. And Jesus didn't leave. He said: don't be afraid.

You don't have to push Him away. He's not going anywhere.

en.verse: And so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus said to Simon. “From now on you will catch men.”
en.note:
You feel too unworthy to have any purpose. Who would use someone like you?

We often think purpose belongs to people who have it together.

Right after Peter said "I'm a sinful man," Jesus said: don't be afraid; from now on you will fish for people. He gave Peter a calling in the same breath as his confession.

Your sense of unworthiness doesn't cancel your purpose. Sometimes it's the doorway to it.

en.verse: The son declared, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
en.note:
You've rehearsed your apology a hundred times. All the ways you've failed, all the reasons you don't deserve forgiveness.

We often prepare speeches about our unworthiness, as if we have to prove we know how bad we are.

In Jesus' story, the son who wasted his inheritance came home with his speech ready: Father, I have sinned. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

If you've been rehearsing your failures, look at what the father does in the next verse.

en.verse: But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.’
en.note:
You're expecting to be put in your place. Treated like a servant, not a child. Accepted, maybe, but on probation.

After failing, we often expect a lesser place.

The father in Jesus' story doesn't let his son finish the speech. He says: quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Not a servant's clothes. A son's.

Whatever speech of unworthiness you've prepared, the Father is already running toward you with a robe.

en.verse: But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’
en.note:
You don't feel spiritual enough to pray. You can barely look up.

We often think prayer requires a certain level of holiness.

In Jesus' story, a tax collector stood at a distance. He wouldn't even look up to heaven. He beat his chest and said: God, have mercy on me, a sinner. And Jesus said he was the one who went home right with God.

You don't need to have it all together. Mercy is for people who know they need it.

en.verse: But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God.
en.note:
You feel like you have to earn your place in God's family. Be good enough, faithful enough.

We often treat belonging as something to achieve.

John writes: to all who did receive Him, He gave the right to become children of God. A right. Not a reward, not something earned. Given.

If you feel unworthy, remember: belonging to God isn't a prize for good behavior. It's a gift.

en.verse: Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?
en.note:
Your past is messy. You've done things, and people know about them. You feel defined by it.

When our failures are known, we often hide or shrink.

The Samaritan woman had a complicated past. Jesus knew all of it and told her so. And instead of hiding, she ran back to her town and said: come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Being fully known and still welcomed made her bold.

You're fully known and still welcomed. Let that make you a little braver today.

en.verse: The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.
en.note:
There's a voice in your head that says you're not enough. Not good enough, not worthy, not loved.

That inner critic can be loud and persistent.

Paul writes: the Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children. When your own voice says you're not enough, there's another voice saying: you're a child of God.

Listen for that voice today. It's quieter, but it's truer.

en.verse: We have different gifts according to the grace given us. If one’s gift is prophecy, let him use it in proportion to his faith.
en.note:
You don't have the gifts other people have. You're not a leader, not a speaker, not artistic.

We often compare our gifts to others' and decide ours don't count.

Paul writes: we have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. Different, not better or worse.

You don't have to have someone else's gift. What's one thing you do that others find helpful? That's a gift. Use it today.

en.verse: Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth.
en.note:
You feel ordinary. Not particularly smart, not powerful, not from an impressive background.

We often assume significance is reserved for the extraordinary.

Paul reminds the church in Corinth: think of what you were when you were called. Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were influential; not many were of noble birth.

Most of the people God chose were ordinary. If you feel ordinary, you're in the majority of the chosen.

en.verse: For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?
en.note:
You feel pressure to prove your worth. To produce value, to justify your existence.

That pressure can be exhausting and never-ending.

Paul asks: what do you have that you did not receive? Everything good in you was given.

That takes the pressure off. You don't have to produce your own worth. It was given to you. You just get to use it.

en.verse: But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design.
en.note:
You feel like you don't fit anywhere. Like you're an accident, a leftover piece.

Feeling misplaced is lonely and discouraging.

Paul writes: God has placed the parts in the body, every one of them, just as He wanted them to be. You're not an accident or an afterthought.

You were placed exactly where you are, on purpose. Your role matters to the whole.

en.verse: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
en.note:
You'll never be good enough. You've tried, and you always fall short.

Perfectionism and shame often say: try harder, do better. But it's never enough.

Paul writes: God made Him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God. Not trying to be righteous. Becoming it, through Him.

When you feel like you'll never be good enough, remember: it was never about you being enough on your own.

en.verse: You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.
en.note:
You feel like a second-class believer. Others seem more spiritual, more devoted.

We often rank ourselves in spiritual hierarchies.

Paul writes to the Galatians: you are all children of God through faith in Christ Jesus. All. No ranking, no tiers. The newest believer and the oldest saint are equally children.

You don't need to climb a ladder. You're already in the family.

en.verse: He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will.
en.note:
You wonder if God really wants you, or if He's just putting up with you.

Many people believe they're tolerated rather than truly wanted.

Paul writes: in love He predestined us for adoption, in accordance with His pleasure and will. Adoption is a choice. Someone chose you, on purpose, with pleasure.

You weren't taken in reluctantly. You were wanted.

en.verse: For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God.
en.note:
You're terrified of losing God's love if you mess up. So you're always trying, always anxious.

When love feels conditional, we live in constant fear of failing.

Paul writes: it is by grace you have been saved, through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God. Not from yourselves. That's the relief.

You don't have to earn it, keep earning it, or worry you'll lose it by not being enough. It's a gift.

en.verse: Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is.
en.note:
You look at yourself and see everything unfinished. Flaws, failures, areas where you're not who you want to be.

We often judge ourselves by where we are now, as if it's the final version.

John writes: dear friends, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been made known. You're not finished. Who you'll become is still being written.

Don't judge yourself by a draft. The final version hasn't been revealed yet.

en.verse: For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.
en.note:
You feel like an embarrassment. Like if people really knew you, they'd be ashamed to be associated with you.

Shame often whispers that we're too much, too broken, too flawed.

The writer of Hebrews says: Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters. Not ashamed. Of you. With all your flaws and failures.

Jesus isn't embarrassed to be associated with you. He calls you family. Proudly.

en.verse: Because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.
en.note:
You feel like you're failing because you're not perfect yet. Still struggling, still growing.

We often think we have to be finished to be acceptable.

The writer of Hebrews says: by one sacrifice He has made perfect forever those who are being made holy. Perfect, and still being made holy. Both true at once.

You're accepted completely, and you're still growing. You don't have to be finished to be fully loved.

en.verse: Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
en.note:
You're not the loud type. Not pushy, not assertive. And in a world that rewards boldness, you feel overlooked.

Quiet people often feel like they don't measure up.

Jesus said: blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. The meek, the gentle, the quiet ones. Not the loudest or most impressive.

If you're not the type to push yourself forward, Jesus calls you blessed. The earth is your inheritance.

en.verse: Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him.
en.note:
You call people, and they don't call back. You reach out, and nothing comes back.

When our reaching out goes unanswered, it deepens loneliness.

David writes: know that the LORD has set apart His faithful servant for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him. Every time.

When you're lonely, the hardest part is often that no one hears you. This verse is quiet and sure: you're heard.

en.verse: Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age.
en.note:
You feel forgotten. Like you've slipped from everyone's mind.

Being forgotten is one of loneliness's quietest pains.

David prays: remember, LORD, Your great mercy and love, for they are from of old. He asks God to remember His own kindness.

You can pray this today. You're not asking for something new, just for what's always been true: His mercy and love, from long ago, still toward you.

en.verse: The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry.
en.note:
No one leans in to listen to you. People hear you, but they're distracted, half-paying attention.

Being half-heard can feel almost as lonely as not being heard at all.

David writes: the eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are attentive to their cry. Attentive: leaning in, the way you lean toward someone you really want to hear.

When no one seems to lean in to listen to you, God does.

en.verse: My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance.
en.note:
Since things got hard, people have stepped back. Friends who used to be close now keep their distance.

Illness and hard times can make people pull away. It hurts, and it's real.

David writes: my friends and companions avoid me because of my wounds; my neighbors stay far away. He doesn't pretend it doesn't hurt.

If people have stepped back from you, you're not imagining it. And you're not alone in it. Someone else has felt exactly this and written it down.

en.verse: Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.
en.note:
Someone you trusted turned on you. A close friend, someone you shared your life with.

Betrayal by a friend is one of the deepest kinds of loneliness.

David writes: even my close friend, someone I trusted, one who shared my bread, has turned against me. Jesus quoted this verse about Judas at the Last Supper.

Betrayal by a close friend is a wound Jesus knows from the inside. You're not alone in it.

en.verse: For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend.
en.note:
The person who hurt you wasn't an enemy. It was someone close. And that makes it so much worse.

Hurt from people we trust cuts deeper than hurt from strangers.

David writes: if an enemy were insulting me, I could endure it. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion, my close friend. The pain is sharper because it's someone he trusted.

This psalm puts it into words. You can pray it as yours.

en.verse: I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to my mother’s sons.
en.note:
You feel like an outsider in your own family. Different, misunderstood, not really belonging.

Family estrangement is a particular kind of loneliness.

The psalmist writes: I am a foreigner to my own family, a stranger to my own mother's children. It's in the Bible, and you're allowed to feel it.

You're not a stranger to God. You belong to Him, even when you don't feel like you belong at home.

en.verse: You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion.
en.note:
You feel completely alone, like darkness is your only company.

Some loneliness is so deep that hope feels out of reach. If it has gone on for a long time, please reach out to someone today: a friend, a doctor, a counselor. You deserve company in this.

This is the last line of Psalm 88, the saddest psalm: You have taken from me friend and neighbor; darkness is my closest friend. No happy ending. Just honest loneliness, offered to God.

If that's how you feel, you can pray it too, word for word. Even your darkest words are heard.

en.verse: I am a friend to all who fear You, and to those who keep Your precepts.
en.note:
You're lonely, and you're not sure where to find people who share what you care about.

Finding friends with shared values can be hard, especially as adults.

The psalmist writes: I am a friend to all who fear You, to all who follow Your precepts. Faith comes with friends: people who care about the same things.

If you're lonely, maybe there's a community nearby where you'd find those people. Look for them this week.

en.verse: You know when I sit and when I rise; You understand my thoughts from afar.
en.note:
You feel unseen. Like no one notices your ordinary moments: when you get up, when you sit down, when you're tired.

We crave being noticed in the small things, not just the big ones.

David writes: You know when I sit and when I rise; You perceive my thoughts from afar. Every small movement of your day is known.

When you feel unseen, remember: someone notices when you get up in the morning, when you sit down at night. You're watched over with care.

en.verse: If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me, and the light become night around me”— even the darkness is not dark to You, but the night shines like the day, for darkness is as light to You.
en.note:
You want to disappear. Hide in the dark where no one can see you, where you don't have to try anymore.

When loneliness is deep, part of us wants to vanish. Being unseen feels safer than being seen and rejected.

David writes: if I say, surely the darkness will hide me, even the darkness will not be dark to You; the night will shine like the day. You can't disappear from His sight. Not even in the dark.

You're visible, even when you're hiding. And seen with kindness, not judgment.

en.verse: How precious to me are Your thoughts, O God, how vast is their sum! If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand; and when I awake, I am still with You.
en.note:
You wonder if anyone thinks about you. If you cross anyone's mind during the day.

We all want to know someone is thinking of us.

David writes: how precious to me are Your thoughts, God! Were I to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand. When I awake, I am still with You. God thinks about you more than there are grains of sand. And every morning when you wake, He's still there.

You're never left. You're on His mind.

en.verse: Look to my right and see; no one attends to me. There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul.
en.note:
You've looked around, and there's no one. No one on your side, no one who cares.

That sense of total isolation is one of the most painful human experiences.

David wrote this hiding in a cave from Saul: look and see, there is no one at my right hand; no one is concerned for me. No refuge, no one who cares. And in the very next verse: I cry to You, LORD; You are my refuge.

If you feel this today, you're in the same place David was. And he found a refuge. So can you.

en.verse: Do not forsake your friend or your father’s friend, and do not go to your brother’s house in the day of your calamity; better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away.
en.note:
Your family is far away. And when things get hard, there's no one close by to lean on.

Distance from family can leave us vulnerable and alone when we most need support.

This proverb says: better a neighbor nearby than a relative far away. When family is far, the people near you can become family.

Who's close by that you could get to know better? A neighbor, a coworker, someone you see every day? Reach out to one of them this week.

en.verse: Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?
en.note:
You feel cold. Not physically, but emotionally. No warmth, no closeness, no one to share life with.

Loneliness has a temperature. It feels cold.

The writer of Ecclesiastes observes: if two lie down together, they will keep warm. But how can one keep warm alone? We're made for warmth with others.

If you're cold today, let someone in, even a little. A phone call, a shared meal, a hug. Warmth starts small.

en.verse: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.
en.note:
You've been rejected, and it feels like no one could understand how much it hurts.

Rejection is deeply isolating. It can make us feel uniquely unwanted.

Isaiah describes a servant who was despised and rejected, a man of suffering, familiar with pain, someone people turned away from. Christians have long read this as a description of Jesus.

When you feel rejected, you're not explaining it to someone who's never felt it. He's been there.

en.verse: No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride.
en.note:
Loneliness has given you a name. Forgotten. Abandoned. Unwanted. And you've started to believe it.

The labels we give ourselves in lonely seasons can stick.

God says through Isaiah: no longer will they call you Deserted. You will be called Hephzibah, which means "my delight is in her." God changes the name loneliness gave you.

You're not Deserted. You're His delight. Try wearing that name today.

en.verse: And they will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD; and you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.
en.note:
You feel left behind. Everyone else has moved on, and you're still here, alone.

Being left behind can make us feel forgotten.

Isaiah says: you will be called Sought After, the City No Longer Deserted. Sought after. Someone came looking for you.

If you feel left behind, this is your new name. You're the one being searched for.

en.verse: As a shepherd looks for his scattered sheep when he is among the flock, so I will look for My flock. I will rescue them from all the places to which they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness.
en.note:
You've drifted away. Lost in the fog, unsure how to get back.

Sometimes loneliness comes from wandering: slowly drifting from people, from God, from ourselves.

God says through Ezekiel: as a shepherd looks after his scattered flock, so will I look after My sheep. I will rescue them from all the places where they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness. Lost in the fog. And the shepherd comes looking.

You don't have to find your way back alone. You're being looked for.

en.verse: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).
en.note:
You feel like God is somewhere else. Watching from a distance, maybe, but not here with you.

We often imagine God as far away, especially when we're lonely.

The whole Christmas story is summed up in one name: Immanuel, which means God with us. Not above, not watching from far away. With.

Wherever you are today, God is with you. That's what His name means.

en.verse: Then Jesus returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asked Peter.
en.note:
You needed people to show up, and they didn't. They were busy, distracted, asleep.

Being let down by friends when we need them most is a deep hurt.

On the night before His death, Jesus asked His closest friends to stay awake with Him while He prayed. He came back and found them sleeping. Couldn't you keep watch with Me for one hour?

He knows what it's like to need people who don't show up. He understands your loneliness from the inside.

en.verse: Then everyone deserted Him and fled.
en.note:
Everyone left. When things got hard, they all walked away.

Total abandonment is one of the most painful experiences there is.

When Jesus was arrested, everyone deserted Him and fled. Everyone. All His friends ran. He was completely alone.

That's why He can be with you in yours. He's been more alone than you'll ever be. You're not alone in your abandonment.

en.verse: And as they talked and deliberated, Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them.
en.note:
You're walking through your days alone, sad, not noticing much around you.

When we're grieving or lonely, we often don't notice who's near.

Two disciples were walking to Emmaus, discouraged after the crucifixion. And Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them. They didn't recognize Him at first.

Someone might be walking beside you today that you haven't noticed yet. Look around.

en.verse: “Come and see,” He replied. So they went and saw where He was staying, and spent that day with Him. It was about the tenth hour.
en.note:
You want to be invited somewhere. Asked over, included, welcomed.

Not being invited is a quiet kind of loneliness.

Two people asked Jesus where He was staying. He didn't give them an address. He said: come, and you will see. And they spent the rest of the day with Him.

Jesus' answer to curiosity is an invitation to company. You're invited too.

en.verse: “You are a Jew,” said the woman. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.)
en.note:
You feel like you're avoided. Like people keep their distance from you.

Being avoided can make us feel like we're somehow untouchable.

The Samaritan woman came to draw water alone at noon, perhaps to avoid other people. Jews and Samaritans didn't associate. And Jesus started a conversation with her. She was shocked: how can You ask me for a drink?

He seeks out the ones others avoid. You're not too far outside for Him.

en.verse: The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
en.note:
You feel like just another face. No one knows your name, your story, who you really are.

Being anonymous in a crowd can be deeply lonely.

Jesus describes Himself as a shepherd: He calls His own sheep by name and leads them out. Not "hey you," not a number. By name.

When you feel like just another face, remember: you're known by name. Someone says it with care.

en.verse: I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me.
en.note:
You want to be known. Really known. Not just the surface, but the real you.

Being truly known is one of our deepest needs.

Jesus says: I am the good shepherd; I know My sheep and My sheep know Me. Known, and knowing back. That's the opposite of loneliness.

A relationship where you're fully seen is offered to you today.

en.verse: As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love.
en.note:
Love feels temporary. People come and go. You're afraid to settle into any relationship.

When love has been unstable, we often stay guarded.

Jesus says: as the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Now remain in My love. Remain: stay, make yourself at home.

Love isn't a visit. It's a place to live. When you feel alone, you can stay in that love.

en.verse: With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart.
en.note:
You're lonely in your faith. No community, no one to share it with.

Faith can feel isolating without others to share it.

The first Christians met every day and shared meals in each other's homes with glad and sincere hearts. Faith was never meant to be lonely. It was meant to be shared at a table.

Who could you share a meal with this week? Faith grows at tables.

en.verse: ‘For in Him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are His offspring.’
en.note:
You feel cut off from everything. From people, from God, from meaning.

Loneliness can make us feel like we're outside of everything.

Paul said this to strangers in Athens, quoting their own poets: in Him we live and move and have our being. You're never outside God. Every breath, every step, you're within His presence.

You can't be alone in that sense. You're held, even now.

en.verse: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?
en.note:
You're afraid something will separate you from love. Distance, failure, circumstances.

Fear of losing love can make us anxious and guarded.

Paul asks: who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or hardship or danger? And the answer, a few verses later: nothing. Nothing in all creation.

No loneliness, no rejection, no distance can separate you from that love.

en.verse: If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.
en.note:
You're suffering, and you're doing it alone. You haven't told anyone.

We often hide our pain, thinking we'll burden others.

Paul writes: if one part suffers, every part suffers with it. You're part of a body. When you hurt, others are meant to feel it too.

If you're suffering alone, maybe it's time to let the body know. Tell someone today.

en.verse: And: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”
en.note:
You don't have the family you wish you had. Maybe they're gone, distant, or just not what you needed.

Family wounds create a deep loneliness.

Paul quotes God's promise: I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters. Whatever family you have or don't have, you have this one.

A Father who claims you. You belong somewhere.

en.verse: Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.
en.note:
You feel like a guest everywhere. Polite, welcome enough, but never really at home.

Not belonging anywhere is a lonely way to live.

Paul writes: you are no longer foreigners and strangers, but fellow citizens with God's people and members of His household. Household. Family.

You're not a guest who has to be polite and leave. You live here. You belong.

en.verse: Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy.
en.note:
You miss someone. A friend far away, someone you used to be close to.

Missing someone is a sign of love. But it can also be lonely.

Paul wrote this from prison to his young friend Timothy: recalling your tears, I long to see you, so that I may be filled with joy. He missed him. And he said so.

Who do you miss today? Tell them.

en.verse: Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.
en.note:
You're lonely, and you're waiting for someone to reach out to you.

Sometimes loneliness eases when we reach out to someone else who's alone.

The writer of Hebrews says: do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it. Abraham did exactly this.

Who's a stranger near you who might need a welcome? Reaching out might ease your loneliness too.

en.verse: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.”
en.note:
You wonder if loneliness will always be part of your life.

When loneliness lasts, it can feel permanent.

Revelation describes the end of the story: God's dwelling place is now among the people, and He will dwell with them. Not us going far away to God. God coming to live with us. Forever.

Loneliness has an expiration date. Hold onto that today.

en.verse: When Jacob woke up, he said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.”
en.note:
You feel alone in a strange place. Far from home, far from anyone who knows you.

Being somewhere unfamiliar can make loneliness sharper.

Jacob was running away from home, sleeping alone on the ground with a stone for a pillow. He dreamed of a ladder to heaven. And he woke up and said: surely the LORD is in this place, and I was not aware of it.

You might be more accompanied than you know.

en.verse: After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself.
en.note:
You long for a deep friendship. Someone who really gets you, who's loyal through everything.

That kind of friendship is rare, and longing for it is natural.

After David defeated Goliath, Jonathan, the king's son, became one in spirit with David, and loved him as himself. One of the great friendships in the Bible. Deep, loyal, lifelong.

If you're lonely, it's okay to hope for that kind of friend. Pray for one today.

en.verse: When the young man had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone, fell facedown, and bowed three times. Then he and Jonathan kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more.
en.note:
You've lost a friendship. Through distance, change, or circumstances. And you're grieving it.

We don't always recognize the loss of a friendship as grief. But it is.

David and Jonathan had to part because Jonathan's father, King Saul, wanted David dead. They kissed each other and wept together, but David wept the most.

If you've lost a friend, your grief is valid. They wept too.

en.verse: I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.
en.note:
You've come through something hard, and you're grateful to be on the other side.

Gratitude after hardship is often deeper than gratitude in easy times.

Psalm 13 starts with "how long will You forget me?" four times. And it ends with this: I will sing the LORD's praise, for He has been good to me. Gratitude at the end of a hard road.

Look back at a hard season today and notice: He was good to me. Let that become a song.

en.verse: To raise my voice in thanksgiving and declare all Your wonderful works.
en.note:
You've noticed good things, but you've kept them to yourself.

Gratitude grows when it's shared. Saying it out loud makes it real.

David writes about proclaiming aloud Your praise and telling of all Your wonderful deeds. Telling. Sharing.

Tell someone today about something good that happened. Saying it makes it real, and might lift them too.

en.verse: Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together.
en.note:
You're grateful, and you want to share it. But you're not sure who to tell.

Gratitude is better shared. When we tell others what we're thankful for, joy multiplies.

David invites: glorify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together. Together. Not alone.

Call a friend today and tell them what you're thankful for. Ask them what they're thankful for. Magnify it together.

en.verse: For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light.
en.note:
Something good happened, and you want to know where it came from.

Tracing good things back to their source deepens gratitude.

David writes: for with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light. Every good thing flows from somewhere.

Today, trace one good thing back to its source. A meal, a friendship, a sunrise. Let it lead you to thanks.

en.verse: Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.
en.note:
You've been complaining a lot lately. And today you want to try something different.

Gratitude sometimes requires letting go of something: a complaint, a grudge, a sense of entitlement.

The psalm says: sacrifice thank offerings to God. A sacrifice costs something. Sometimes gratitude costs attention, time, or giving up a complaint.

Make a small thank offering today. Stop and say thanks when you'd usually rush past or grumble.

en.verse: You attend to the earth and water it; with abundance You enrich it. The streams of God are full of water, for You prepare our grain by providing for the earth.
en.note:
It rained today, or it's going to. And instead of being annoyed, you're trying to see it differently.

We often overlook the gifts in weather, in nature, in ordinary cycles.

This harvest psalm says: You care for the land and water it; You enrich it abundantly. The streams of God are filled with water to provide the people with grain.

Next time it rains, try saying thank you. It's watering something.

en.verse: Come and listen, all you who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for me.
en.note:
Something God did for you is on your mind. You're grateful, and you think someone else might need to hear about it.

Our stories of gratitude can encourage others who are struggling.

The psalmist invites: come and hear, all you who fear God; let me tell you what He has done for me.

Is there something God did for you that you could share? Someone might need to hear it today.

en.verse: The earth has yielded its harvest; God, our God, blesses us.
en.note:
You're eating a meal, and you suddenly realize how many hands went into it.

Every meal is the result of countless people's work: farmers, drivers, cooks.

This psalm says: the land yields its harvest; God, our God, blesses us. Every meal is a harvest.

Before your next meal, pause and think about where it came from. Say thanks for the land, the workers, and the One who blesses the harvest.

en.verse: I will praise God’s name in song and exalt Him with thanksgiving.
en.note:
Things aren't perfect, but you're grateful anyway. And that surprises you.

Gratitude in the middle of trouble is powerful. It doesn't deny the trouble. It just refuses to let it have the final word.

Psalm 69 is mostly a cry of distress: waters up to the neck. And yet, near the end, it turns into this: I will praise God's name in song and glorify Him with thanksgiving.

Thanksgiving doesn't wait for everything to be fixed. It can rise from the middle of trouble.

en.verse: My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long.
en.note:
You've been noticing good things all day. Small things, but they're adding up.

The more we pay attention to good things, the more we see.

The writer of this psalm was old, looking back on a whole life: my mouth is filled with Your praise, declaring Your splendor all day long. All day long.

What if you tried noticing good things all day today? Keep a running count. You might be surprised.

en.verse: I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart; I will glorify Your name forever.
en.note:
You say thank you a lot, but usually on autopilot. Today you want to really mean it.

Quick, automatic thanks is good manners. Wholehearted thanks is something deeper: slowing down to really feel it.

David writes: I will praise You, Lord my God, with all my heart. Not half-heartedly. Not with a distracted "thanks." All my heart.

Pick one thing today and be fully, wholeheartedly grateful for it. Sit with it for a minute. Let it fill you.

en.verse: Sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done wonders; His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory.
en.note:
Something new and unexpected happened. A surprise, an answer you didn't see coming.

New blessings deserve fresh gratitude, not the same tired words.

The psalmist calls out: sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done marvelous things. A new song for new wonders.

What's something new God has done recently? Something you didn't expect? That deserves a fresh thank you. Maybe even a new way of saying it.

en.verse: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth. Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs.
en.note:
You're grateful, but you feel self-conscious about showing it. It feels silly to be too happy.

Many of us hold back joy, afraid of seeming over the top.

This psalm invites: shout for joy to the LORD, all the earth. Worship the LORD with gladness; come before Him with joyful songs. Not a perfect noise. A joyful one.

Gratitude doesn't need to be polished. Sing badly today. Laugh loudly. Be glad. No one's grading you.

en.verse: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, You are very great; You are clothed with splendor and majesty.
en.note:
You stepped outside and something caught you: the light, the sky, the trees. And you felt small and glad at the same time.

Noticing creation is one of the oldest ways of practicing gratitude.

Psalm 104 is a whole hymn of noticing. It begins: praise the LORD, my soul. LORD my God, You are very great. And then it describes mountains, rivers, birds, wine, bread, the moon, the sea.

Go outside today and notice. Then bless. Let the bigness of the world make you grateful.

en.verse: Wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine, and bread that sustains his heart.
en.note:
You're enjoying something simple: a good meal, a warm shower, a comfortable bed. And you feel almost guilty for how good it is.

Simple pleasures are gifts. We don't have to apologize for enjoying them.

The psalmist lists them: wine that gladdens human hearts, oil to make their faces shine, and bread that sustains their hearts. Good food, small luxuries. All part of the goodness of creation.

Enjoy one of them fully today. Taste it. Say thank you. Simple pleasures are part of the design.

en.verse: Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations.
en.note:
You're grateful for something, and you want to tell the world.

Gratitude naturally wants to be shared. When we tell others, it spreads.

This psalm opens: give praise to the LORD, proclaim His name; make known among the nations what He has done. Make known. Spread it around.

Share one thing you're thankful for today: with a friend, in a note, wherever it fits. Let your gratitude travel.

en.verse: Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.
en.note:
You've been rescued from something. Maybe recently, maybe long ago. And you want to remember it.

Remembering past rescues is one of the strongest foundations for gratitude.

Psalm 107 tells four stories of rescue: wanderers in the desert, prisoners in darkness, the sick near death, sailors in a storm. After each one, the same line: let them give thanks to the LORD for His unfailing love and His wonderful deeds.

What have you been rescued from? Every rescue deserves a thank you.

en.verse: Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them.
en.note:
You're amazed by something. How the world works, how the body heals, how the stars move. And the wonder makes you grateful.

Wonder and gratitude are close cousins. Being amazed often leads to thanks.

This psalm says: great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them. This verse is carved over the doorway of a famous old physics laboratory in Cambridge, England. Scientists studying the universe, delighting in its design.

Let something amaze you today. Wonder is a kind of gratitude.

en.verse: I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD.
en.note:
You want to be grateful, but something is in the way. A grudge, a complaint, a sense that you deserve more.

Gratitude sometimes requires letting go of something.

The psalmist says: I will sacrifice a thank offering to You. A sacrifice is something you give up.

What could you set down today in exchange for thanks? A complaint, a grudge, a comparison? Let it go, and see what gratitude fills its place.

en.verse: You are my God, and I will give You thanks. You are my God, and I will exalt You.
en.note:
You're grateful not just for what you have, but for who God is.

Some gratitude goes beyond gifts. It's thanks for a relationship, for presence.

The psalmist says it twice, like a vow: You are my God, and I will praise You; You are my God, and I will exalt You. Gratitude rooted in relationship.

You are my God. That's enough to be thankful for, even before anything else.

en.verse: At midnight I rise to give You thanks for Your righteous judgments.
en.note:
It's the middle of the night, and you can't sleep. Instead of worrying, you want to try something different.

Sleepless nights often fill with worry. But they can also fill with gratitude.

The psalmist writes: at midnight I rise to give You thanks. Gratitude at midnight.

When you can't sleep, instead of worrying, try counting good things. Midnight thanks can turn a restless night into a peaceful one.

en.verse: They will extol the fame of Your abundant goodness and sing joyfully of Your righteousness.
en.note:
You've been focused on what's lacking. Today you want to see the abundance instead.

We tend to notice gaps more than fullness. Shifting focus takes intention.

The psalmist writes: they celebrate Your abundant goodness and joyfully sing of Your righteousness. Abundant: overflowing, more than enough.

Today, try to see the abundance in your life instead of the gaps. There's more good than you usually notice.

en.verse: Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving; make music on the harp to our God.
en.note:
You're grateful, but words don't quite capture it. You need something more.

Music often expresses what words can't. It opens the heart.

The psalmist calls: sing to the LORD with grateful praise; make music to our God on the harp.

Put on music today that makes you grateful. Sing along. Let music carry your thanks where words don't reach.

en.verse: Praise Him, O sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars.
en.note:
You're looking up at the sky, and you feel a quiet thankfulness for simply being part of it all.

Creation itself seems to praise just by existing, by being what it was made to be.

The psalmist calls on everything to praise: praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all you shining stars. Even the sky gives thanks just by shining.

Look at the sky tonight if you can. Let the stars remind you: everything that exists is a reason for gratitude. Including you.

en.verse: Now therefore, our God, we give You thanks, and we praise Your glorious name.
en.note:
You're looking back over a long stretch of life, and you feel grateful for how far you've come.

Looking back can reveal blessings we didn't notice in the moment.

David prayed this near the end of his life, after gathering gifts for a temple he would never see built: now, our God, we give You thanks, and praise Your glorious name. Looking back on everything, his big prayer was thanks.

What would your thank-you prayer be, looking back? Say it today.

en.verse: You alone are the LORD. You created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them. You give life to all things, and the host of heaven worships You.
en.note:
You're breathing, alive, here. And you realize that's a gift.

Life itself is so constant that we forget it's given, not owned.

This prayer was spoken by the people of Jerusalem after they'd rebuilt the city walls: You give life to everything. Every living thing, including you, is sustained.

Your next breath is a gift. Take a slow breath right now and say thank you.

en.verse: But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. I will fulfill what I have vowed. Salvation is from the LORD!
en.note:
You're in a hard spot, but something in you still wants to give thanks.

Gratitude in a difficult place is powerful. It doesn't deny the difficulty. It looks beyond it.

Jonah prayed this from inside a great fish: with shouts of grateful praise, I will sacrifice to You. Salvation comes from the LORD. Not after being rescued. During.

If you're in a hard spot, try thanking anyway. Gratitude in an impossible place can be the most honest kind.

en.verse: O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You; I will praise Your name. For You have worked wonders—plans formed long ago—in perfect faithfulness.
en.note:
Things came together in a way you didn't plan. And now you can see how it all worked out.

Sometimes we only see the pattern in hindsight.

Isaiah writes: LORD, You are my God; I will exalt You, for in perfect faithfulness You have done wonderful things, things planned long ago. Some good things in your life were planned long before you saw them.

Look back and notice: how did things come together? That's faithfulness. Thank Him for it.

en.verse: I will make known the LORD’s loving devotion and His praiseworthy acts, because of all that the LORD has done for us—the many good things for the house of Israel according to His great compassion and loving devotion.
en.note:
You want to remember all the good things, so you don't forget them when hard times come.

Writing down blessings creates a record we can return to.

Isaiah begins: I will tell of the kindnesses of the LORD, the deeds for which He is to be praised, according to all the LORD has done for us. He starts listing.

Try it today: list everything good God has done for you. Start with this week. Then go back further.

en.verse: Then Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior!”
en.note:
Something unexpected has come into your life, and you're not sure how it'll turn out. But part of you is grateful anyway.

Gratitude doesn't always wait for clarity. Sometimes it comes first.

Mary sang this when she was young, poor, unmarried and newly pregnant. Not an easy situation. And her first response was: my soul glorifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.

Gratitude can come before everything is clear. Let it come today.

en.verse: The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.
en.note:
Something wonderful happened, and now you're going back to ordinary life.

After a high point, returning to routine can feel flat.

After seeing the newborn Jesus, the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things they had heard and seen. They went back to their ordinary jobs, but changed.

Gratitude doesn't take you out of normal life. It changes how you live it. Carry today's thanks back into the ordinary.

en.verse: Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted.
en.note:
What you have seems small. Not enough. And yet you're grateful for it.

Gratitude for the little we have can open the door to more.

Five thousand people were hungry, and all they had was five loaves and two fish. Not nearly enough. Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them. He gave thanks before the miracle, for the little He had.

Thank God for what's small today. It might grow.

en.verse: So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me.”
en.note:
You're waiting for an answer, and you want to trust it'll come. Can you be grateful before you see it?

Thanking in advance is a kind of trust.

At Lazarus' tomb, before Lazarus came out, Jesus looked up and said: Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. Thanks in advance.

Gratitude can be a kind of trust: thanking God before you see the answer. Try it today with something you're waiting for.

en.verse: After he had said this, Paul took bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat.
en.note:
Everyone around you is anxious. And you want to bring a little steadiness.

Gratitude can be contagious. When one person gives thanks in a hard moment, it can steady others.

Paul was on a ship in a storm for two weeks. Everyone was terrified and hadn't eaten. Paul took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, and began to eat. And they were all encouraged.

Your thanks might steady someone else today.

en.verse: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!
en.note:
Something hard is still ahead, but you know how the story ends. And that makes you grateful.

Gratitude for the ultimate outcome can carry us through present struggles.

Paul ends his chapter on resurrection: thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Victory over death itself.

Whatever you're facing today, the ultimate victory is already won. Let that be your reason for thanks.

en.verse: All this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.
en.note:
You're grateful, and you notice it seems to be spreading. Others around you are lighter too.

Gratitude is contagious. When we're thankful, it affects those around us.

Paul writes: all this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is reaching more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow.

Your thanks today might start a chain reaction. Let it overflow.

en.verse: Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful.
en.note:
You want to notice more good things. But you're always so busy that you miss them.

Gratitude is a habit of attention. It requires looking.

Paul writes: devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful. Watchful: looking for things to be thankful for.

Keep your eyes open today. Good things are hiding in plain sight. Catch a few.

en.verse: For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected.
en.note:
You feel guilty for enjoying good things. As if pleasure is somehow wrong.

Some of us learned that enjoying life is selfish or unspiritual.

Paul writes: everything God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. Food, rest, pleasure, beauty: all good when received with thanks.

You don't have to feel guilty enjoying good things today. Just say thank you.

en.verse: Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe.
en.note:
Everything else is shifting, but you're grateful for something that doesn't change.

In uncertain times, gratitude for stable things anchors us.

The writer of Hebrews says: since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful. Unshakable. When everything else feels unsteady, there's something that can't be moved.

That's worth being thankful for. Rest your gratitude on it today.

en.verse: Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.
en.note:
You want gratitude to be more than an occasional feeling. You want it to be a way of life.

Gratitude grows when it becomes a habit, not just a reaction.

The writer of Hebrews says: let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise. Continually. Not just on good days.

Try ending today by naming three good things, no matter what kind of day it was. Do it again tomorrow. That's how gratitude becomes a way of life.
